state.misconception_label: Assumes that an arrow on a number line starts at zero

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I have: ![Number line with -12 and -7 marked. Starting at -12, follow an arrow pointing to the right labelled +10. Then there is an arrow labelled b pointing to the left, which ends at -7 on the number line.]() What is the value of \( b \) ? I got \( -7 \) because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Imagine you were moving objects along a number line. If you start at -12 and move 10 units to the right, then move some units to the left to end up at -7, what would the value of \( b \) be in this situation?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Okay, so if I start at -12 and move 10 units to the right, I think I get to -2. But then I have to move left to end at -7. So, how far do I need to move left from -2 to get to -7? I'm not sure how to figure that out.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Imagine you were sliding objects along a number line. If you start at -12 and move 10 units to the right to reach -2, how many units would you need to slide to the left to end up at -7? Would your method still give the right answer if you were physically moving objects along the number line?

score.justification_pass1: The teacher effectively addresses the misconception by emphasizing starting position through concrete movement scenarios, and the student successfully corrects their understanding by Turn 2 (recognizing -12 as the starting point and reaching -2), though the teacher's final turn is somewhat repetitive rather than helping with the remaining calculation.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher consistently uses concrete physical analogies (moving/sliding objects along a number line) to ground the abstract mathematical concept, though the analogies are somewhat repetitive and could have been more varied or deeply connected to everyday situations.
